1

Philanthropy Concentration in Quebec & Canada

CRA T3010 charity returns — 83,727 charities, $421.9B aggregate revenue

Research objective

Every registered Canadian charity files a T3010 annual return with the CRA, and the CRA publishes the whole filing in bulk. That gives us a near-complete census of the third sector — name, sector, province, revenue, expenses, assets, donations, compensation — for every registered organisation in the country. The same concentration dynamics that play out in private-sector industries (a long tail with a fat head) almost certainly hold for Canadian philanthropy too, but no one has a clean, public-facing view of it for Quebec. An insight here unlocks targeted advice for foundation clients (where to deploy dollars for marginal impact), pro-bono partners (which underserved sectors need capacity), and policy stakeholders (how Quebec's nonprofit ecosystem compares structurally to the rest of Canada).

Key questions teams can explore

  • What share of Quebec charitable revenue is held by the top 1% of charities? Top 10%? (Lorenz / Gini view)
  • How does the size distribution differ between Quebec, Ontario, and BC?
  • Which CRA sectors are over- or under-represented in Quebec vs. the national average?
  • Where is the gap between number of organisations and revenue captured the largest?
  • What does the long tail look like — how many Quebec charities operate on less than $100K / year?
  • Which sectors have the highest tax-receipted donations as a share of revenue (most dependent on individual donors)?
  • Where would a $10M strategic grant land in the size distribution — transformative, or rounding error?
  • How does Montreal-region concentration differ from rest-of-Quebec?
Dataset
CRA T3010 Registered Charity Information Return (2024 bulk)
PublisherCanada Revenue Agency, via Government of Canada Open Data
Size33 MB across 2 CSVs + 2 PDFs (data dictionary + codes lookup)
Shape83,727 charities × 200+ T3010 line items; join key BN (15-char Business Number)
VintageFiscal year 2024, last refreshed May 2026
LicenceOpen Government Licence — Canada
How to download it yourself
  1. Open the open-data dataset page — https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/80c00cdb-1358-415c-bb8b-0de7f12675b8
  2. Scroll down to the Resources section
  3. Click Charities Identification (CSV, ~13 MB) — one row per registered charity
  4. Click Charities Financial (CSV, ~21 MB) — one row per filing with all T3010 line items
  5. Optional: download the Data Dictionary PDF and Codes Lookups PDF for variable definitions
  6. Save all four files to a data/ folder next to your script

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • Provincial bar chart — count of registered charities by province, Quebec called out
  • Quebec sector-mix donut — share of Quebec charitable revenue by CRA category (Core Health Care and Teaching Institutions dominate)
  • Lorenz-style concentration curve — cumulative revenue captured vs. cumulative charity count, Canada vs. Quebec overlaid
  • Plus four summary CSVs: headline_summary.csv, by_province.csv, quebec_by_sector.csv, summary_tabulations.csv
Headline finding from the starter analysis
Quebec is the most concentrated major province: the top 100 Quebec charities hold 78.9% of all Quebec charitable revenue (vs. 57.9% in Ontario). Core Health Care + Teaching Institutions account for ~$66B of Quebec's $87B in charitable revenue.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • T3010 line 4700 ("revenue") includes government transfers — for a university or hospital, most of that is provincial funding, not philanthropic donations. Use line 4500 (tax-receipted gifts) when the question is specifically about donor dollars.
  • Self-reported, not audited — a few charities mis-code their category or report zeros where they shouldn't.
  • Address is the registered head office — a national charity headquartered in Montreal will count as Quebec even if 80% of programs run elsewhere.
  • No demographic / beneficiary data — T3010 says what the org does, not who it serves. Census tables are the natural pair.
2

Montreal Rental Housing Affordability

Census FSAs × CMHC 2025 + GIS layer — 196 FSAs mapped, 34.5% cost-burdened, downtown stress cluster visible

Research objective

Housing affordability in Montreal has deteriorated sharply since 2020. CMHC's 2025 Rental Market Report puts year-over-year asking-rent growth at roughly 11% across the Montreal CMA, while incomes (Census 2020) lag far behind. This kit lets a small team quantify cost-burden at a neighbourhood level (Forward Sortation Area, FSA), identify the most-exposed geographies, and link the affordability picture to landlord-side rent dynamics from CMHC's primary rental survey. The output is directly useful for pro bono support to Ville de Montréal, FRAPRU, the Société d'habitation du Québec, or community housing organizations.

Key questions teams can explore

  • Which Montreal FSAs have the highest share of cost-burdened renters (≥30% of income on shelter)?
  • Where is the situation severe (≥40% of renters cost-burdened, or ≥50% of income on shelter)?
  • How well do CMHC RMS rent zones align with Census FSAs, and where do the two sources disagree on "expensive" neighbourhoods?
  • Which neighbourhoods have BOTH high rent and high cost-burden (high rent alone can signal a high-income enclave, not stress)?
  • Which demographic groups (one-parent families, seniors, recent immigrants) are most concentrated in stressed FSAs?
  • What is the relationship between % subsidized tenant housing and overall cost-burden?
  • Has rent grown faster than median income since the 2016 census?
Dataset
StatsCan Census 2021 FSA Profile + CMHC Rental Market Survey 2025
PublisherStatistics Canada (Catalogue 98-401-X2021013) + Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
SizeCensus subset: 645 KB (filtered from 645 MB national CSV); CMHC: 245 KB xlsx
Shape196 Montreal-area FSAs × 21 metrics + 23 CMHC zones × bedroom-type × 2 years
VintageCensus 2021 income (2020 reference year); CMHC October 2025
LicenceStatistics Canada Open Licence; CMHC public data
How to download it yourself
  1. Census FSA — start at the StatsCan profile download tool — https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2021/dp-pd/prof/details/download-telecharger/comp/page_dl-tc.cfm?Lang=E
  2. Pick Geographic level: Forward Sortation Area, then Download CSV (English) — file 98-401-X2021013 (~68 MB zip)
  3. Unzip and filter to Montreal-area postal codes: H* prefix (island + Laval) plus J3T, J3X, J3Z, J4*, J5*, J6*, J7* (South Shore + North Shore)
  4. CMHC — direct xlsx download of the 2025 Montreal Rental Market Report — https://assets.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/sites/cmhc/professional/housing-markets-data-and-research/housing-data-tables/rental-market/rental-market-report-data-tables/2025/rmr-montreal-2025-en.xlsx
  5. Open the xlsx and look at Table 1.1.2 — average rent by zone and bedroom type, Oct 2024 vs. Oct 2025

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • FSA choropleth map — 195 Montreal-area FSAs coloured by % of renters cost-burdened; downtown cluster (H3A/H3B/H3G/H3H) at 54–64% jumps out immediately
  • Small-multiples panel — 3-up map: cost-burden, median renter shelter cost, median household income, same geography
  • Top stressed FSAs bar chart — H3B Downtown Montreal leads at 63.5% of renters cost-burdened
  • Plus the joined mtl_fsa_joined.geojson (ready for hackathon teams to extend in geopandas, folium, or kepler.gl) and affordability_tabulations.csv
Headline finding from the starter analysis
34.5% of Montreal-area FSAs have at least 30% of their renter households cost-burdened. Worst FSA is H3B (downtown) at 63.5% of renters cost-burdened — McGill/Concordia student zone with median rents of $1,500–1,740 against student-level incomes. CMHC 2BR average rent ranges from $1,057 to $2,092 across the 23 Montreal CMA zones, with 10.9% YoY rent growth 2024 → 2025.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • Geographic mismatch — CMHC RMS uses 23 survey zones; Census uses ~200 FSAs in the Montreal CMA. They aren't nested. A true join requires a Census-Tract crosswalk.
  • Time lag — Census shelter-cost and income data reflect 2020/2021; CMHC rents are October 2025. Implied real-time STIR is higher than the Census figure.
  • All-household income, not renter income — true renter STIR is meaningfully higher than the all-household proxy.
  • Small-sample FSAs — a few outliers (J4X, J7B, H3Y) have very few tenant households (<700) and high reported STIR; treat as noisy.
3

Food Insecurity and Food Bank Usage in Quebec & Canada

StatsCan + HungerCount 2024 — the Quebec prevalence-vs-reach paradox

Research objective

Quantify the scale, growth, and demographic profile of food insecurity and food bank usage in Quebec relative to the rest of Canada — and identify where the gap between food insecurity prevalence (a household-survey measure) and food bank reach (an operational measure) is widest. The intent is to produce evidence that a pro bono team could hand directly to Banques alimentaires du Québec to sharpen targeting, advocacy, and capacity planning.

Key questions teams can explore

  • How has Quebec's food insecurity prevalence evolved 2018–2024, versus Canada and other provinces?
  • Quebec has ~22% of Canada's population but ~35% of national food bank visits in March 2024 — what explains the over-indexed visit rate despite a lower survey-measured prevalence?
  • Which household types (one-parent families, persons not in an economic family) are most over-represented in Quebec's food-insecure population?
  • Children are 35% of Quebec food bank visits vs. 33% nationally — what does the Quebec age curve (0–5 cohort especially) tell us about young-family vulnerability?
  • Where is the gap between prevalence and reach largest, and what does that say about access, stigma, or referral patterns?
  • Which provinces saw the steepest post-pandemic visit growth (2019–2024), and how does Quebec's +109% compare?
Dataset
StatsCan Tables 13-10-0834 & 13-10-0835 + Food Banks Canada HungerCount 2024
PublisherStatistics Canada (Canadian Income Survey) + Food Banks Canada
SizeStatsCan: ~3 MB across two CSVs; HungerCount: 2.7 MB PDF + two transcribed CSVs
Shape1,624 prevalence rows (6 regions × demographic × year) + 10 provinces × visits/age
VintageFood insecurity 2018–2024; HungerCount March 2024 snapshot
LicenceStatistics Canada Open Licence; Food Banks Canada (publication is public)
How to download it yourself
  1. Open StatsCan Table 13-10-0835 (food insecurity by demographic) — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1310083501
  2. Click Download options → CSV (all years, current configuration)
  3. Repeat for Table 13-10-0834 (by economic family type) — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1310083401
  4. Download the HungerCount 2024 PDF ("Buckling Under the Strain") — https://fbcblobstorage.blob.core.windows.net/wordpress/2024/10/hungercount-2024-en.pdf
  5. Provincial table is on page 23 — either parse with pdfplumber/tabula-py or transcribe the 12-row table by hand (it's small)

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • Prevalence trend line — food insecurity % over 2018–2024, Quebec vs. Canada vs. other regions
  • Provincial bar chart — March 2024 food bank visits per province, child share called out
  • Demographic breakdown — Quebec vs. Canada deltas by household type (one-parent, senior, single-person)
  • Plus summary_by_province.csv joining HungerCount visits to StatsCan prevalence with per-capita rates
Headline finding from the starter analysis
Quebec has lower survey-measured food insecurity (18.0% in 2024) than the national average (24.0%), yet accounts for 35% of all Canadian food bank visits despite being ~22% of population. Quebec's per-capita food bank visit rate (79 per 1k) is 1.6× the national rate. The starter exposes this paradox — solving it is the hackathon puzzle.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • HungerCount measures visits (a single client can drive many); StatsCan measures household prevalence from the Canadian Income Survey. Don't mix without caveat.
  • The Quebec prevalence-vs-reach paradox is real but unresolved — could reflect stronger Quebec food-bank density, more frequent visits per client, or measurement differences.
  • StatsCan 13-10-0835 collapses geography to 6 regions plus Canada (no Alberta-only, no PEI-only).
  • Pre-2024 HungerCount provincial tables would strengthen the trend story but require extracting from older PDFs.
4

Montreal Climate Vulnerability — Heat Islands × Demographics

GIS theme — Ville de Montréal heat layer overlaid on borough income & seniors

Research objective

This is the GIS-heavy theme, ideal for teams who want to leverage Cursor on real-world geospatial analysis with geopandas, polygon overlays, and choropleth mapping. The starter overlays the City of Montreal's 2023 satellite-derived urban-heat-island layer onto arrondissement boundaries and a parsed 2021-census poverty / age profile to identify the boroughs whose populations are most exposed to combined climate-and-equity risk. The seed output is a single vulnerability choropleth that a Ville de Montréal climate-adaptation team could use to prioritise tree-canopy and cooling-centre investment.

Key questions teams can explore

  • Which Montreal arrondissements combine high heat-island exposure with high concentrations of seniors 65+ (most at risk of heat-related mortality)?
  • Which neighbourhoods sit at the intersection of low income and high heat exposure, where private adaptation (AC, mobility) is hardest?
  • How does the 2023 heat-island footprint compare with 2013 / 2016 baselines — where is the city heating up fastest?
  • Where would investment in tree canopy yield the largest equity-weighted reduction in heat exposure?
  • Are existing municipal cooling assets (pools, libraries, parks) located inside the most heat-vulnerable polygons, or mis-aligned with need?
  • How does the borough-level picture change at dissemination-area / census-tract resolution (stretch goal)?
Dataset
Ville de Montréal heat-island GeoJSON + arrondissement boundaries + parsed borough poverty profiles
PublisherVille de Montréal (Données Montréal portal), Statistics Canada 2021 Census (custom order)
Size~35 MB total — heat-island raw GeoJSON 18 MB + cleaned GeoJSON 15 MB + boundaries 1.5 MB + parsed CSV + 19 HTML reports
Shape5 heat classes × city polygons; 19 arrondissement polygons; per-borough % low-income, % seniors, population
VintageHeat: 2023 summer satellite; demographics: 2021 Census
LicenceCC-BY 4.0 (Ville de Montréal); Statistics Canada Open Licence
How to download it yourself
  1. Arrondissement boundaries — Données Montréal — https://donnees.montreal.ca/dataset/limites-administratives-agglomeration
  2. On the dataset page, download the GeoJSON resource (NAD83 / MTM 8, EPSG:32188)
  3. Urban heat islands 2023 — Données Montréal — https://donnees.montreal.ca/dataset/ilots-de-chaleur
  4. Download the heat-island GeoJSON (it's actually Esri JSON wearing a .geojson extension — convert with build_heat_geojson.py in this folder)
  5. Borough demographic profiles — https://donnees.montreal.ca/dataset/portrait-thematique-sur-la-pauvrete-2021
  6. Download the 19 borough HTML reports and parse % low-income (MBM), % seniors 65+, and total population — the starter does this for you with a regex parser

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • Vulnerability choropleth — 19 boroughs coloured by equal-weighted z-score of (heat exposure × % low-income × % seniors); top-5 labelled
  • Raw heat-island map — 2023 hot-pixel polygons overlaid on borough outlines
  • Top-10 ranked bar chart — borough vulnerability scores with the three driver values stacked
  • Plus vulnerability_by_arrondissement.csv with full 19-row z-score breakdown
Headline finding from the starter analysis
The vulnerability index ranks Anjou and Saint-Léonard highest — 1960s east-end boroughs with ~20% seniors and large asphalt/flat-roof footprints — followed by Ville-Marie (22.9% low-income downtown) and Le Plateau-Mont-Royal (densest urban fabric, 100% heat exposure). West Island and L'Île-Bizard sit at the low-vulnerability end.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • Heat-island data is satellite surface temperature, not lived air temperature — overcounts industrial roofs and asphalt that aren't necessarily where residents live.
  • Demographic data is borough-level (19 polygons) — masks huge intra-borough variation. Census-tract redo is the natural stretch goal.
  • The 2023 image was captured during a heat wave, so absolute heat-island extent is on the high end of the 2013–2023 series.
  • Index uses equal-weighted z-scores of three drivers — defensible starting point, but teams should challenge the weights.
  • Both layers are in EPSG:32188 — do NOT reproject to lat/lon before computing areas.

Healthcare Access in Quebec — Wait Times & Regional Disparities

MSSS ER feeds + StatsCan — 17 RSS regions, 5 fiscal years, live occupancy

Research objective

Quebecers wait longer for emergency care and are less likely to have a family doctor than other Canadians — but the within-Quebec story is sharper than the cross-Canada one. Stretcher length of stay ranges from ~9 hours in Bas-Saint-Laurent to ~20 hours in Montréal, Laval and Laurentides, and several RSS hospitals operate at over 100% stretcher occupancy on any given day. For the Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux (MSSS), regional CISSS/CIUSSS boards, and McKinsey's Canadian healthcare practice, the question is not whether Quebec underperforms in aggregate (it does) but which regions drive the gap, and what the relationship is between primary-care attachment and downstream ER pressure.

Key questions teams can explore

  • Which Quebec RSS regions have the longest ER stretcher length of stay, and which run consistently above 100% stretcher occupancy?
  • How does Quebec compare to Ontario, Alberta, and BC on the share of residents with a regular healthcare provider?
  • Has Quebec's gap vs. the rest of Canada widened or narrowed 2015–2022?
  • What share of Quebec ER patients are on a stretcher for more than 24 hours, and how does that vary by region?
  • Where would adding 100 family-medicine slots have the biggest predicted ER deflection?
  • How concentrated is ER strain — what % of "stretcher-hours over 24h" sits in the four GMA RSS (Montréal, Laval, Laurentides, Montérégie)?
Dataset
MSSS ER feeds (cumulative + live snapshot) + StatsCan T13-10-0096
PublisherMinistère de la Santé et des Services sociaux du Québec + Statistics Canada
SizeMSSS cumulative 196 KB; MSSS hourly 25 KB; StatsCan 4.7 MB zip
Shape802 RSS-fiscal-year rows × 27 ER metrics + live per-installation occupancy + provincial healthcare characteristics
VintageMSSS FY 2022-23 through 2026-27 (partial); StatsCan 2015–2022
LicenceDonnées Québec open data; Statistics Canada Open Licence
How to download it yourself
  1. MSSS Fichier cumulatif des urgences — Données Québec — https://www.donneesquebec.ca/recherche/dataset/fichier-cumulatif-des-donnees-des-urgences
  2. Click the CSV resource — it's a small file (~200 KB) refreshed each MSSS period
  3. MSSS Relevé horaire des urgences (live snapshot) — https://www.donneesquebec.ca/recherche/dataset/fichier-horaire-des-donnees-de-la-situation-a-l-urgence
  4. Download the CSV; note it's latin-1 encoded with trailing whitespace in column names
  5. StatsCan Table 13-10-0096 healthcare characteristics — direct CSV zip — https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/tbl/csv/13100096-eng.zip
  6. Unzip and load the main CSV (the zip contains a 4.9 MB CSV plus metadata files)

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • Provincial family-doctor bar chart — 10-province ranking of "has a regular healthcare provider %", Quebec called out
  • Quebec RSS ER stays — stretcher length-of-stay by region for the latest cumulative period
  • ER occupancy vs. volume scatter — today's live stretcher occupancy plotted against annual visit volume, one dot per RSS
  • Plus summary_quebec_access.csv with one row per RSS (visits, % >24h on stretcher, mean LOS, live occupancy)
Headline finding from the starter analysis
Quebec ranks 2nd-lowest in Canada on family-doctor coverage (78.7%) vs. 10-province average 84.8% — a 6.1 pp gap. But the bigger story is intra-Quebec: mean stretcher LOS ranges from 9.4h (Bas-Saint-Laurent) to 19.9h (Montréal) — a 2.1× spread. Live snapshot today shows Laval at 161% stretcher occupancy, Montérégie 129%, Outaouais 124%. The story is regional, not provincial.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • Live snapshot drifts — the hourly file reflects ER status at the moment of download, so reruns will yield different fig3 outputs.
  • StatsCan T13-10-0096 is province-level only. INSPQ regional indicators would close the gap but require manual portal scraping (stretch goal).
  • MSSS reports cumulative-since-April; the latest year (2026-27) is a partial period and not directly comparable to closed years.
  • Visits are raw counts, not per-capita — normalising by RSS population would change the ranking (Côte-Nord, Gaspésie look small in volume but heavy per-capita).
6

Montreal Public Safety — SPVM Crime Patterns

SPVM Actes criminels — 351,687 incidents 2015–2026, mapped to 19 arrondissements

Research objective

The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal publishes one of Quebec's richest open-data files: every reported criminal incident from 2015 forward, with lat/lon, category, date, and time-of-day. That gives a Montreal team a near-complete spatial view of where and when crime concentrates across the 19 arrondissements. The same data is consumed by SPVM's own strategic planning, by community-safety organizations, and increasingly by social-services agencies who use crime patterns to position outreach. A pro bono team could deliver a per-capita risk map, identify under-resourced or over-stressed neighbourhoods, or link crime patterns to housing and income data to expose where physical insecurity compounds with economic vulnerability.

Key questions teams can explore

  • Which arrondissements have the highest per-capita crime rate, and is the ranking stable across 2015–2024?
  • How does the crime mix differ between downtown (Ville-Marie, Plateau, Sud-Ouest) and the west island?
  • Which categories are growing fastest and which are declining over the decade?
  • How does crime intensity correlate with neighbourhood income? (cross-link with Theme 2 FSA affordability data)
  • When are the worst hours and days? (QUART = jour / soir / nuit breakdown)
  • What share of incidents have privacy-blanked lat/lon, and does that systematically bias the choropleth?
  • How does Ville-Marie's daytime commuter population distort the per-resident rate, and what would a daytime denominator change?
Dataset
SPVM Actes criminels (incidents reported by Montreal police)
PublisherService de police de la Ville de Montréal, via Données Montréal
Size30 MB CSV — 351,687 incident rows
ShapePer-incident: category, date, QUART (shift), PDQ (police district), lat/lon
Vintage2015-01-01 to 2026-06-12 (refreshed continuously)
LicenceCC-BY 4.0 (Ville de Montréal open data)
How to download it yourself
  1. Open the SPVM Actes criminels dataset page on Données Montréal — https://donnees.montreal.ca/dataset/actes-criminels
  2. In the Resources section, click the CSV resource (file is typically actes-criminels.csv)
  3. If curl hits an RBAC denial, add a browser User-Agent: curl -A 'Mozilla/5.0' -O ...
  4. Save to data/spvm_actes_criminels.csv
  5. For arrondissement boundaries, reuse Theme 4's GeoJSON or download from Données Montréal — https://donnees.montreal.ca/dataset/limites-administratives-agglomeration

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • Per-capita crime choropleth (hero) — 19 arrondissements coloured by crimes per 1,000 residents; Ville-Marie at 44.1 jumps out from the west-island tail near 5
  • Top categories bar chart — Vol dans véhicule, Méfait, and Vol de véhicule lead the 2024 mix by far
  • Time series 2015–2024 — top 3 categories overlaid; reveals pre-pandemic baseline, COVID dip, post-2022 recovery
  • Plus crime_by_arrondissement.csv joining population, total crimes, per-capita rate, and top category for each borough
Headline finding from the starter analysis
Ville-Marie at 44.1 crimes per 1,000 residents is the downtown outlier — inflated roughly 3× by daytime commuter population. The next tier (Plateau-Mont-Royal 20.5, Sud-Ouest 18.5) forms a downtown-adjacent hot zone. West-island arrondissements (Pierrefonds-Roxboro 5.7, L'Île-Bizard 5.0) and Outremont 7.7 sit at the cool tail. Across the decade the category mix has shifted steadily toward property crime.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • Privacy-blanking — roughly 17% of incidents have lat/lon set to (0, 0) by SPVM for anonymization. The starter drops these before the spatial join, which may systematically understate location-sensitive categories like sexual assault.
  • Ville-Marie's per-resident rate is inflated by daytime commuter population — a daytime denominator would soften the spike.
  • Villes liées (Westmount, Mont-Royal, Hampstead, etc.) are not in the demographics file used and render grey on the choropleth.
  • Crime categorization has evolved mid-decade — pre-2018 and post-2018 categories aren't perfectly comparable.
7

Quebec EV Adoption and the Energy Transition

SAAQ + Circuit Électrique — 167,940 EVs in 2022, 43.6% CAGR, 23.6 EVs per public charger

Research objective

Quebec is North America's leading EV-adoption jurisdiction by share of new-vehicle registrations, and the SAAQ publishes vehicle-in-circulation data at the régionale-administrative level with the powertrain field populated. Combined with the Circuit Électrique public charging network registry, that gives a hackathon team a near-real-time view of where adoption is concentrating, where the charging infrastructure gap is widest, and which regions are on or off the provincial 2030 trajectory. Direct relevance for McKinsey's automotive and energy practices, for Hydro-Québec's electrification planning, and for the Ministère de l'Économie's industrial-policy decisions on battery and charging investment.

Key questions teams can explore

  • Which Quebec regions are leading and lagging on EV share of total light-duty stock?
  • Where is the charging-infrastructure gap (EVs per public charger) most acute?
  • What is Quebec's compound annual growth rate, and where would the linear trajectory land in 2030?
  • How is the mix shifting between battery-electric (VEÉ) and plug-in hybrid (VHR)?
  • How does Quebec compare to BC and Ontario on EV penetration?
  • Which regions are over- or under-served by the Circuit Électrique network relative to their EV stock?
  • What does a 2027 capacity plan need to look like to keep EV-per-charger ratios from doubling again?
Dataset
SAAQ Véhicules en circulation + Le Circuit Électrique charging stations
PublisherSociété de l'assurance automobile du Québec + Hydro-Québec's Le Circuit Électrique, via Données Québec
SizeSAAQ aggregated: 7.5 KB (from ~250 MB streamed per year); Circuit Électrique: 1.5 MB
ShapeEV stock by region × powertrain × year (2018 + 2022 in starter) + 7,109 Quebec charging stations with lat/lon, type, kW
VintageSAAQ 2018 and 2022 snapshots; Circuit Électrique current as of download
LicenceOpen Government Licence — Québec (CC-BY 4.0)
How to download it yourself
  1. SAAQ Véhicules en circulation on Données Québec — https://www.donneesquebec.ca/recherche/dataset/vehicules-en-circulation
  2. Each year's resource is a ~250 MB CSV streamed from S3 — use the included aggregate_saaq.py as a template (streams + aggregates without persisting raw)
  3. Circuit Électrique stations — Données Québec dataset — https://www.donneesquebec.ca/recherche/dataset/circuit-electrique-bornes-de-recharge
  4. Or direct CSV from Le Circuit Électrique's own data portal — https://data.lecircuitelectrique.com/
  5. Save aggregated outputs to data/saaq_ev_by_region.csv and data/circuit_electrique_stations.csv

Expected outputs — what the starter kit produces

  • EV growth trend — Quebec light-duty EV stock 2018 → 2022, VEÉ (battery) and VHR (plug-in hybrid) shown separately
  • Regional EV penetration bar — top 10 regions by EV share of light-duty stock; Montérégie and Lanaudière lead at 4.0%
  • Charging station map — 7,109 Circuit Électrique stations across Quebec, sized by kW or coloured by Niveau 2 vs. BRCC fast DC
  • Plus ev_summary_by_region.csv with EV count, total stock, EV share, and EVs-per-charger for all 17 regions
Headline finding from the starter analysis
Quebec light-duty EV stock grew from 39,456 (2018) to 167,940 (2022) — a 43.6% CAGR and 4.3× expansion in four years. The mix is shifting toward battery-only (61% in 2022, up from 47% in 2018). But the network is straining: EVs per public charger went from 5.8 to 23.6 — a 4× pressure increase. Laval is the worst-served leader at 64.7 EVs per charger vs. Montréal's 11.3.
Known data limitations to flag with the team
  • BEV vs. PHEV definitional drift — SAAQ's fuel-type coding has changed mid-decade; pre-2017 records often lack a clean powertrain field.
  • Stock not flow — these are vehicles in circulation, not new registrations; momentum lags policy by 12–24 months.
  • Region = registered owner's residence, not where the vehicle is driven. A Montréal commuter registered in Lanaudière counts as Lanaudière.
  • Circuit Électrique only — Tesla Supercharger, FLO, ChargePoint, and ServiceON networks are not in the dataset (likely 20–30% under-count).
  • SAAQ release lag — the latest published snapshot is typically about 12 months behind, so 2025 figures land in mid-2026.
  • No vehicle-kilometres-travelled denominator — EVs may drive less per car than ICE, so stock share overstates emissions reduction.

How to use this catalogue on Friday

  1. Pick a theme — open the corresponding folder under ~/Desktop/mck_hackathon_montreal/
  2. First 15 minutes — read the theme README, run python3 analysis.py, open the baseline PNGs in outputs/
  3. Next 90 minutes — pick one or two "suggested analyses" from the README and extend the starter
  4. Last 15 minutes — each team shares one chart and one sentence
